abstract: High-frequency circuit and system designers now have an important new tool in their arsenal of technologies. Monolithic gallium-arsenide (GaAs) digital ICs have emerged, bringing with them the promise of multigigabit and higher data rates beyond the reach of present silicon-based integrated circuits. Applied to future systems, the new circuits would go a long way toward slashing the size, weight, and eventually the cost of high-frequency electronic equipment -and, in the process, vastly enhancing the capabilities of equipment spanning the commercial and military worlds.

articleTitle: Communications: One way to talk to computers: Voice commands to computers may substitute in part for conventional input devices
abstract: No longer the province of science fiction, machines that recognize and interpret spoken commands are now a commercial reality — and have been for more than three years. Fortunately for the human ego, such machines cannot (as yet) take over the operator's task. They do not really understand the words, but merely recognize them and perform preprogrammed assignments in response. The benefit of a simple system of this type is that it can be “taught” to recognize any language or accent. In other words, the machine is trained to understand the user — not the other way around.

articleTitle: Two-way communication for load management: The results of system tests now underway will guide utilities in performance, cost, and legal aspects
abstract: Two-way communications systems are now offering the potential of sophisticated techniques for load management. These systems also are bringing automation in power distribution closer to realization through automatic and remote reading of kilowatthour meters, and through their ability to monitor and control power distribution networks.

Monolithic integrated-circuit chips that convert voice to digital signals are now being sold, breadboarded, and designed, and use of these chips on a massive scale, in telephone equipment and systems, is imminent. The chips are called codecs (coder-decoders) and the long-term design vision is a codec in every telephone handset. Telephone engineers and integrated-circuit designers generally feel that widespread handset use is still beyond the horizon, but codecs clearly have a vital role to play in the oncoming era of digital telephone.

articleTitle: Graphics displays: Factors in systems design
abstract: Most applications call for individualized computer-graphics system design using “off-the-shelf” subsystem building blocks In image processing, architectural design, cockpit simulation, artist-console operation, and process control, users can turn to large computer-graphics systems that come complete with all the necessary hardware and software (see “Graphics displays,” Aug., p. 24). But much more common is the case in which a set of unique requirements calls for individualized computer-graphics system design.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Announcing the Amazing Micro-Mouse Maze Contest
abstract: It was through mere happenstance that Spectrum's editors learned — by means of word propagated along the industry grapevine — of a so-called electronic mouse (“le mouse electronique” were the exact words that reached our ears). Upon assigning our top investigative reporters to the task of finding out the true facts, we quickly found that in January the magazine Machine Design had indeed called for designers and constructors of “electronique” mice to enter The Great Clock Climbing Contest. Contestants would be required to construct a mechanical mouse that could attempt to climb a vertical mesh screen (“le clock,” one supposes). Our disappointment came when it was hinted the mice would merely be battery-powered and, probably, electric-motor driven. No electronics here, our purist minds concluded.

articleTitle: Where and when to use which data converter: A broad shopping list of monolithic, hybrid, and discrete-component devices is available; the author helps select the most appropriate
abstract: With the commercial availability of data-converter products — the result of both hybrid (multichip) and monolithic (single-chip) technologies — users of analog-to-digital (A/D) and digital-to-analog (D/A) converters now have an impressive array of designs from which to choose. In addition, the older discrete-component designs still remain a viable choice for many high-performance applications, particularly those where broad operating characteristics and specialized features are important. Unfortunately, rather than helping the users to match the proper products to their needs, data-converter manufacturers confuse the issue by arguments over the relative merits of the different technologies. A closer look at the various types of data converters may help to clear up some of this confusion.

The complexity and cost of making analog measurements can be reduced by the use of a microprocessor. In an analog instrument, the microprocessor not only can absorb many digital control functions, but it can also reduce analog circuitry drastically - if new analog techniques that take advantage of the microprocessor's power are utilized. Reducing the analog portion of the instrument is important, even at the expense of adding more digital circuitry, because precision analog components are expensive and adjusting, testing, and troubleshooting analog circuits is costly. Often, digital circuits can replace analog circuits because various functions can be executed in either mode. By using a microprocessor, many of these functions can be programmed in software rather than executed in hardware, either analog or digital.

articleTitle: Solid-state devices: Amorphous semiconductors revisited: Despite residual skepticism, they've been successfully used in memory, microfiche, and graphic-arts applications
abstract: A noted silicon semiconductor authority recently remarked: “Many semiconductor experts who doubt the usefulness of amorphous semiconductor technology haven't given the technology a second, more recent look. Don't criticize what you haven't seen.”

articleTitle: Electronics in medicine: A mixed blessing: Technology does lots more, but at a price
abstract: According to a recent study by the U.S. Department of Health, Education and Welfare, health-care costs in the United States will rise 40 percent by 1980 — to $224 billion a year. A Congressionally enacted national health insurance program could raise this figure by an additional $9.8—$24.8 billion, depending upon which program under consideration is adopted. Medical technologies are contributing to these rising costs in several ways. For example, some technologies require large capital investments; others necessitate costly supporting services; and still others dictate expensive follow-up care. In fact, it has been estimated that 50 percent of the increase in costs of hospital care from 1965 to 1974 was due directly or indirectly to medical technology.

articleTitle: Unjamming traffic congestion: Computer-based systems can speed traffic, increase safety, and improve gasoline mileage
abstract: “If we can land a man on the moon, then we should be able to find a green light on our roads when we need it” may be the way a frustrated driver caught in a traffic tieup sees things. But to traffic engineers, the sentiment reflects widely held myths concerning what even the latest equipment — computer-based traffic-control systems — can reasonably do and what it cannot.

articleTitle: Power semiconductors: Looking ahead: Consumer applications will grow for moderate-current devices while large-diameter wafers await packaging innovations
abstract: Starting cautiously with the earliest solid-state diodes and transistors, applications for solid-state power control devices first took off with the commercial introduction of silicon controlled rectifiers (SCRs) in December 1957. Since then, the power-handling capabilities of silicon devices have so improved that 8000-kVA phase-controlled locomotives and high-voltage dc transmission (HVDC) designs deploying 500 MW now use solid-state components. But in terms of potential dollar volume, perhaps the largest growth area for solid-state power devices involves handling the relatively modest power levels associated with home wiring and consumer electronics. New, interesting applications in this area include emergency lighting, static relays, ground-fault circuit interrupters, and home-appliance speed controls. Building code and/or legislative support exists for ground fault interrupter and emergency lighting, while static relays and appliance speed controls are essentially displacement-type markets.

articleTitle: The multifacets of I2L: Exploiting a technique once assumed merely to encourage annoying parasitics, integrated injection logic is burgeoning
abstract: What once was regarded largely as a potentially troublesome parasitic problem — allowing devices to merge into the same semiconductor region of an integrated circuit (IC) — has blossomed into integrated-injection logic (I<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>L), a full-fledged bipolar technology able to compete with older, established technologies in the marketplace.

articleTitle: Communications: The military goes digital: Digital switching and signaling, along with digital transmission, offer reliability in a hostile environment
abstract: For military needs, the smaller size, simpler design, and lower cost of digital switching systems are important features, just as they are in commercial telephone applications. In addition, powerful digital signaling and error-control techniques — available in all-digital telephone systems — provide highly reliable signaling and allow signaling throughput to be maintained in higherror-rate transmission environments.

articleTitle: Computers: All pervasive: Hardware and software progress is steady; Applications continue to expand
abstract: In almost every area of computer engineering, 1976 saw incremental progress, with the accent on refining and using already developed technology, rather than expanding it through new breakthroughs.

articleTitle: Pleasing the consumer while playing to win: Consumer electronics is Japan's trump card — Fine-tuned to woo customers, dispel adversity
abstract: Japan's technical accomplishments maintain a particularly high profile among math students, homemakers, television fans, citizens band radio operators, and audiophiles — in short, everyone who uses consumer electronics. Successful Japanese companies have earned their reputation through exacting attention to product engineering and marketing strategy. The emphasis is on producing a high proportion of technological successes, rather than spectacular but economically unsound “firsts.”

articleTitle: Robots get smarter and more versatile: Robots and computer-based systems proliferate, having gained inroads due to labor shortages
abstract: The high degree of industrial automation in Japan is characterized by an ever-increasing use of robots and computers in production control. In fact, robotry is a full-fledged industry in itself, with some 120 Japanese companies presently manufacturing various types of robots and 1977 sales expected to reach a total of $300 million. Two thirds of this volume involves so-called “low-class” robots — sequentially controlled devices mainly employing techniques such as relay logic or mechanical sequencers. The rest of the market is comprised of “middle-class” robots that have a “playback” or numerical-control capability and employ position coders. In addition, recent models of the latter are being equipped with sensors, making them more adaptable to flexible programming.

articleTitle: The `green wave' rolls on [computerised road traffic control]
abstract: Central computer control is helping the Federal Republic of Germany manage its street and highway vehicular traffic, which has been increasing in volume over the past two decades. Constrained by narrow city streets and squares (many of historical interest) that were incompatible with modern traffic systems, German traffic engineers were forced early to utilize available traffic surfaces to best advantage - mainly by refinements in existing traffic-control systems.

articleTitle: Education: Accreditation: A debatable issue: Key officers of IEEE express diverging views on the role the Institute should play in accrediting electrical engineering programs
abstract: An often-heated debate has raged within IEEE circles for several years over various aspects of accreditation. One major area of concern has been the quality of engineers entering the work force each year. According to many, there has been insufficient attention paid, within IEEE as elsewhere, to the establishment and enforcement of appropriate educational standards in B.E.E. curricula. Further, critics have questioned IEEE's continued endorsement of bachelor of technology programs, suggesting that graduates of such programs are too often accepted by industry as full-fledged EEs. The primary target of such criticisms has been the Engineers Council for Professional Development (ECPD), an umbrella organization that has been the principal arbiter of engineering education standards for nearly 50 years. Its detractors say that ECPD has persisted in stacking its evaluation teams with a predominance of engineering educators who tend to favor relaxed standards. Within IEEE, therefore, there has been an outcry for the Institute to pressure ECPD into reforms of its entire evaluation process — and to withdraw from that body if progress is unsatisfactory.

articleTitle: Banking/commerce: Electronic funds transfer: Too much, too soon? The technology is available but the barriers of regulations, economies of scale, and consumer attitudes must be overcome
abstract: The National Commission on Electronic Fund Transfers, in a recent report to the U.S. Congress, stated that Americans soon will be able to dispense with cash and checks, to a large degree, and turn to computer systems for accommodating funds transfer and bill paying. And, the Commission stressed, they will be able to do so without fear of invasion of their privacy - if Congress enacts some safeguards.

As irony and coincidence would have it, on the opening day of a recent conference at which a retrospective look was taken at local hydroelectric power generation, David Lilienthal, a founding director of the Tennessee Valley Authority and the Atomic Energy Commission's first chairman, writing in the New York Times, proposed that "all over this country there are substantial amounts of renewable sources of electrical energy: the energy in the moving waters of our rivers and waterways. The technology and the manufacturing capability to convert these waters to electricity are here today. No long-range plans or large Federal appropriations or guarantees are needed."

The safety of their product has become the object of serious attention by instrument manufacturers. Among the reasons for this increased interest: the greater use of instruments by nontechnical and unskilled persons; the possibility of lawsuits for liability resulting from injuries and accidents due to unsafe instruments; increasing sales of instruments to overseas markets (some manufacturers report that more than half of their total sales are to overseas customers) where conformity to an internationally acceptable safety standard is important; and gentle prodding by local governments and the Federal government through the Occupational Health and Safety Act (OSHA) for safety certification.

articleTitle: Personal development: Career hurdles and how to clear them: Will an advanced degree and adherence to the work ethic suffice in moving ahead?
abstract: Faced with the myriad suggestions offered them on career development, engineers might well question the effectiveness of the various alternatives. Suggested courses of action have run the gamut from earning a higher degree and obtaining better job assignments to improving one's social skills and developing a “bail-out” option. But with the current scarcity of hard data on how such courses of action affect long-term career development, how can one confidently pursue any approach?

articleTitle: I2L: It's getting faster and smaller
abstract: Semiconductor manufacturers have embarked on a four-pronged effort to enhance the already impressive advantages of I<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>L. High chip-circuit densities and good switching speeds have been further extended as manufacturers tighten design tolerances, simplify device structures, reduce signal swings, and apply dielectric-isolation techniques. The result is to advance dramatically the capabilities of the first bipolar technology to compete seriously with MOS in its strong suit — large-scale integration.

articleTitle: The engineer: A perennial student: Engineers are reminded that the process of learning shouldn't end as the classroom door closes behind them
abstract: Various proposals have been made in recent years to detach engineering colleges from the balance of the university and isolate them in specially organized and separated “Professional Schools of Engineering,” with autonomous control by the engineering faculty of both their membership and curricula. I believe that such proposals are steps in the wrong direction.

articleTitle: Cars and kilowatts: While Detroit remains uncommitted to electric and hybrid vehicles, private industry in Europe and Japan has already taken the plunge
abstract: In February 1974, while delegates from around the world gathered in Washington, D.C., to attend the Third International Electric Vehicle Symposium and Exposition, those who drove to the meeting from nearby suburbia wondered if they could buy enough gasoline to get home. The Arab oil embargo dramatically demonstrated how vulnerable the U.S. transportation system is to even a temporary interruption in petroleum supply. Since then, electric and hybrid vehicles have been getting a hard look from the U.S. Congress and the Department of Energy.

It is difficult to single out one “development of distinction” that, by itself, is representative of the multitudinous accomplishments of the EE profession. However, the following three recent benchmark events are illustrative of EEs' diverse roles.

articleTitle: Automating the production line: Henry Ford began it all when he designed the first car assembly line in 1914
abstract: In the industry that first conceived and implemented the “automated factory,” signs of automation may begin far from the automobile production lines. For example: • New-car orders, received from sales districts over a data-communications network, are keyed into a teletypewriter system that uses computer-stored data to identify accessories, optional equipment, and other distinguishing features that are to be built into each car. When assembled cars leave shipping bays, a controlling and monitoring computer keeps track of their movements.

articleTitle: Communications and microwave technology: in hardware, it's fiber optics and digital radios; in "software," at&t and fcc trade parries
abstract: Covers topics including new FCC rules, fiber-optics experiments, increased bandwidth performance, reduced fiber breakage, non-metalic temperature probes, intersatellite links, MARISAT for maritime applications, and new commercial satellites.

articleTitle: Computers: Computer-based machine-tool control: The best place to inject a computer in numerical control is locally, not as a controller of many systems
abstract: An important advance in the philosophy of numerical control (NC) of machine tools took place during the early 1970s. That advance was the shift toward the use of computers instead of controller units in NC systems, and it produced both computer numerical control (CNC), in which a self-contained NC system for a single machine tool includes a dedicated computer processor controlled by stored instructions to perform some or all of the basic numerical control functions; and direct numerical control (DNC), which refers to a system of several machine tools directly controlled by a central computer.

articleTitle: Electronics in medicine: Imaging technology: A European survey: New devices and techniques provide more revealing images for medical diagnoses
abstract: After a physician talks to a patient and gets a medical history, he may wish to “see” inside the patient's body. Although surgical investigation is sometimes the only way to determine exactly what a medical problem is, or the extent of that problem, physicians are relying increasingly on various electronic diagnostic instruments to extend their senses: Among such instruments are ultrasonic scanners, thermographic devices, radionuclide imaging, endoscopic instruments, and microscopes. But yet another technique — X-ray imaging — has acquired particular popularity. Recent developments, such as computerized three-dimensional image generation and sophisticated digital image-processing systems, together with electronic picture processing, are enabling higher image quality while underscoring the need for an economically viable technology for bulk picture storage.

articleTitle: I The state of the technology
abstract: Electronic funds-transfer (EFT) systems apply electronics technology to common financial transactions, those typically handled by cash or checks. In the process, these systems may also transfer associated information. The principal EFT systems in operation today are: online teller terminals, automated teller machines, point-of-sale devices or terminals, automated clearing-houses, and facilities for paying bills by telephone. All of the technology for these services is here now. Most of the technology necessary to develop additional EFT services is also here now. What the future may bring is improvements in the types of equipment involved, leading to EFT systems providing a wider range of consumer services, and the development of large-scale switching and processing centers to communicate transaction messages from many merchant locations to many different financial institutions.

articleTitle: Balancing clean air against good mileage: Contradictory specifications for lower emissions and improved fuel economy require compromise solutions
abstract: The myth that there is no interaction between automobile emission levels and fuel economy has become imbedded in political debates on future Government requirements. Behind that myth is the argument that, despite tighter emissions requirements, the automobile industry has managed to improve fuel economy over the years.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Japan today: Assets, liabilities, and the future
abstract: O iso gashii densho ga … is a greeting the occasional visitor to Japan may be well advised to master. Freely translated it means, “Please excuse my intrusion; I know you must be in an honorably busy state of affairs …” — a popular salutation that reflects the respect in which the Japanese citizen holds industriousness and the work ethic.

articleTitle: DOE: Outlook on fuel economy: A three-pronged program that could save hundreds of thousands of barrels of oil daily
abstract: Last year in the U.S., the more than 100 million automobiles on the road consumed the equivalent of five million barrels of oil per day. An increase in their fuel economy of just one mile per gallon would have saved the equivalent of 400 000 barrels of oil per day. Because the automobile is the primary petroleum-energy consumer (it not only consumes more petroleum than trucks and buses combined but also more than either the industrial or residential sector), it has been the main focus of the transportation-energy-conservation efforts of the U.S. Energy Research and Development Administration [now part of the Department of Energy (DOE)]. These efforts are aimed at ensuring that technologies are available to reduce petroleum-energy consumption by these vehicles for the near term; and at eliminating their dependence on this diminishing energy resource, while maintaining current mobility levels, in the longer term.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: The bankers vs. technology
abstract: More than a year ago, one of the largest commercial banks in the U.S. installed what it labeled a “Convenience Center” in New York City's Grand Central Terminal. On weekdays, the center opened early and closed late, one objective being to permit dashing commuters to engage in simple banking transactions (deposits and withdrawals) before and after regular business hours. To accomplish this, the center was equipped with one automatic deposit machine (“Instaposit”) and three identical automatic cash-delivery machines. The deposit machine was designed to accept cash or checks in a sealed envelope and return a dated receipt to the customer, while simultaneously depositing the envelope in a locked box. The cash machines were designed to respond to the customer's keyboard request for an envelopeful of cash. The customer simply inserted a magstripe plastic card and entered his personal code number, which was communicated to a central data bank containing the customer's account status. If cleared to make a withdrawal, the customer then punched in a request for $25, $50, $75, or $100, and the machine disbursed the appropriate number of envelopes, each containing two tens and a five.

Several factors helped drive the metropolitan New York area into total blackout on a hot summer night in July. The blackout was reminiscent of the Northeast Blackout of 1965 — although not as widespread, it lasted longer. Investigative teams, including Con Ed's own, have since quickly and accurately analyzed the 53-minute sequence that resulted in complete isolation and shutdown of the Con Ed system. There were no real surprises, except, perhaps, the lightning stroke that started it all by tripping, simultaneously, two circuit breakers on adjacent power lines between Buchanan and Millwood, in Westchester County. Following this, certain equipment did not operate in a satisfactory manner, but in each case the cause or probable cause was diagnosed subsequent to the outage. In any event, these failures to function optimally or at all were in a fail-safe direction, so that equipment was safeguarded. Indeed, one of the criticisms resulting from the investigation relates to the possibility of overly conservative settings and/or inappropriate configurations that voided generating capacity prematurely. Further, it is generally conceded by the investigators that the Con Ed system itself is vulnerable to mishaps because its ties to the outside world are marginal when compared to that of other systems. This situation was compounded at the time of the blackout by an out-of-service intertie between New Jersey and Brooklyn. Finally, the communications among control centers left much to be desired. Much of the information transmitted during the critical period was by informal voice (telephone) communication, some of it ambiguous, unclear, or incomplete.

articleTitle: Technological Japan: Formula for success: The ambition, dedication, and motivation of the Japanese people play an important role
abstract: With a mixture of respect and envy, Japan watchers term this technically advanced country “Japan Inc.” It is a label that Japanese businessmen, particularly those concerned with international trade negotiations, would prefer to see excised from the Westerner's vocabulary. But it will not go away, principally because of the success of the Japanese in producing high-quality, high-technology products that are competitive in the world marketplace. As one Japanese businessman put it, “Japan's problem is that she makes and sells to the West the same products that are made and sold in the West, but more cheaply and of better quality.”

articleTitle: The U.S. promotes electric vehicles: An energy department program is designed to encourage research and support experiments
abstract: On September 17, 1976, the U.S. Congress overrode a Presidential veto, thus giving birth to public law 94–413, the “Electric and Hybrid Vehicle Research, Development, and Demonstration Act of 1976.” The act authorizes a Federally funded program to promote electric and hybrid vehicle technologies and to demonstrate the commercial feasibility of electric and hybrid vehicles. And it calls for a two-part demonstration program under which 7500 such vehicles are to be placed in service on U.S. highways. In addition, a program of financial incentives involving planning grants and loan guarantees to vehicle manufacturers is to be implemented. Directing and monitoring this entire effort is the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE).

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Report from the U.K.
abstract: The energy crisis of 1974 that put many of Britain's electronics companies on a three-day week is now largely forgotten. When memories are pressed, what emerges is that, after all was said and done, productivity during the crisis increased, despite curtailments of the work week and the energy available to do the job. In fact, many recall the crisis with fondness as a difficult challenge met with courage and style.

articleTitle: Fast bonding cuts auto costs: An important development speeds assembly through “welding” of plastic to metal
abstract: A new inductive heating technique for fast bonding of relatively thin metallic — mainly ferromagnetic — parts to nonmetallic components is making inroads in automobile manufacturing. Primarily developed for the very demanding time constraints of the automobile industry's assembly-line environment, this method is characterized by a uniform heat distribution within sharply defined boundaries and by unique, precisely controlled temperature sequences. The present uses of the heating technique — the fastening of plastic retainer clips, the bonding of the manufacturer's identifying “logo” to the car's body, and the bonding of metallic fastening clips to the curved surfaces of glass windows and to the automobile's plastic grill — are just the forerunners of a great many applications.

articleTitle: Autos and public transit: Friends or foes? A “balanced” transportation system would exploit the advantages of both private motor vehicles and public transportation systems
abstract: The role of public transit in a world dominated by the private automobile is a subject that has been marked by controversy, at times bordering on the political. As such, it has been an international concern of Government bodies, consumer groups, and research institutions, as well as individuals. And in an era when the effects of pollution and the energy shortage seem to be catching up with us, the debate assumes a new relevance.

articleTitle: More fun for the consumer: CB explodes and home video games capture the consumer's fancy
abstract: Consumers, always eager for something new, useful, or just plain fun, were served a double helping of technical treats over the past 12 months. Erupting from a highway subculture, citizens band radio became such a hot item during 1976 that on January 1, 1978, the old 23-channel service was broadened to 40 channels in an attempt to alleviate congestion and mutual interference. A second, but no less significant, sensation was the home video game that rang up heavy sales during the 1976 preholiday season, with the promise that even more imaginative, challenging games will be marketed during 1977.

articleTitle: Logic analyzers: A variety of general and special purpose digital circuit analyzers can be used for system development and/or diagnosis
abstract: Digital-circuit hardware and software problems are finding new solutions with the development of new trouble-shooting tools, such as logic and microprocessor analyzers — the result of the increasing use and complexity of digital integrated circuits (ICs). When Spectrum surveyed the logic analyzer field in 1974 (see “The state of logic analyzers,” Dec. 1974), there were only three firms — and a handful of logic analyzer models — on the scene. Today, nearly two dozen companies are producing a multitude of models too numerous to list (see Table I for a representative sampling). The original logic analyzer has spawned bus analyzers, microprocessor analyzers, logic state analyzers, and a variety of other digital-circuit-analyzer instruments.

articleTitle: Communications: Digital and optical: Digital networks are endemic and fiber optics are on the horizon for TV and telecommunications
abstract: Reviews Japanese developments in digital, computer based communication systems including fibre optics.

articleTitle: Railroads: Green light for the bullets: Advances in vehicles, communications, and signals keep plans for the Shinkansen line on schedule
abstract: The Japanese National Railways (JNR) operates as many as 28 000 trains a day on its 21 161-km system. The world's fastest service is offered by JNR on the Shinkansen — literally, the “new trunk line.” Popularly called bullet trains, the Shinkansen cars were first introduced in 1964, when the new line was opened between Tokyo and Shin-Osaka. This was followed by the opening of a section between Shin-Osaka and Okayama in 1972, and an extension to Hakata in 1975 — providing an artery of 1177 km for high-speed travel between Tokyo and Hakata. Traveling time between the two cities is less than seven hours.

articleTitle: Electronics takes control in manufacturing: Computer numerical control excels, lasers invade, and energy is saved
abstract: Energy conservation has become a watchword in industrial electronics — a sector of electronics that has been undergoing a quiet evolution rather than a revolution marked by dramatic breakthroughs. Thus, during the past year, attention has centered on new systems and components aimed at reducing energy consumption, increasing efficiency, and simplifying plant operations.

articleTitle: Looking down the road: A projection of how five major factors will impact the car of tomorrow
abstract: Predictions often appear ludicrous, even shortly after they have been made. Nevertheless, to make sound decisions concerning policies and their implementation, one must consider the range of “probable futures.” Since the automobile plays such a dominant role in U.S. society and economy, it is particularly necessary to consider the future in formulating policies that affect it. Just as Government actions have had a large influence on the development of the automobile transportation system in the past — in areas such as highway construction, vehicle safety standards, emissions control, and fuel economy — so will future Government actions continue to influence the use and characteristics of the automobile.

articleTitle: Military and aerospace: Radars see better; Vikings soar, roost, test, and tell
abstract: From radar to computers and from weapon systems to communication and navigation equipment, technical advances on a broad front marked a year already highlighted by the successful landing of two Viking spacecraft on Mars.

articleTitle: Technology and society: Indonesia is "wired," while U.S. public interest groups "monitor" nuclear technology
abstract: At the interface between technology and society, controversy has come to be expected, but this need not be the case. During 1976, Indonesia - the fifth largest country in the world - bought a communications system. With it, more than 100 million people for whom even telephones have been a rarity were given access not only to telephony, but also to radio and television - and, in turn, to educational and health-care services never before available, particularly in remote areas.

EFT systems offer businesses and individuals a new set of alternatives for conducting their financial transactions. As with any new product or service, success will depend on consumer acceptance in the marketplace. In seeking this success, EFT has to contend with three barriers: regulation, economies of scale, and consumer attitudes. None of these barriers are insurmountable, but they are all sufficiently serious that potential service providers must take them into account in their planning.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Over (or under) 40 and out (or in)
abstract: Listen to this manager speaking: —When crunch time comes, my best engineers help me to try to save the department — my worst people try to save themselves. It's too bad, but it's usually too late for the `losers´ _ who invariably have no trouble in identifying themselves.“ Another manager disagrees ” somewhat. “It's not that simple. There are at least three categories: my best people I really want to keep, the usual deadwood I'm glad to lose, and a whole group in between — good, journeyman engineers who, through no fault of their own, because of external economic conditions, project phase out, or what have you, are forced `on the beach′ for no good reason. It's traumatic for them, for their families, for me, and for the company. Many of these people are in the over-40 category, and feel that they are being singled out because of age and high salary.”

articleTitle: Where the EE works: Is your “cubbyhole,” workbench, or office less than what you'd like it to be? Here are some suggestions
abstract: Cold, hot, stuffy, cramped, poorly lighted, lacking privacy, disruptive to concentrated work effort… these are just a few of the complaints commonly lodged against engineering department “bull pens.” And adding glass-top partitions may only aggravate the situation. In this environment, the privacy game is played with five-drawer file cabinets scattered like pawns throughout the department's checkerboard grid. Stuffed with vendor catalogues and carefully positioned, these monoliths help guard their resourceful owners from continual distraction and exposure.

articleTitle: U.S. shows stage a comeback: A shell game played without a pea, the electronics exhibition is prey to economics and psychology
abstract: On the occasion of its Golden Anniversary, IEEE's premiere annual convention — called INTERCON after the AIEE/IRE merger — passed away, only to be reborn as ELECTRO. Once internationally recognized as one of the largest and most successful conventions and exhibitions of its kind, INTERCON in 1976 gave way to a primarily regional show, ELECTRO, that in alternating years moves between Boston, Mass. (replacing NEREM), and New York City. INTERCON's demise is easy to explain: A virulent disease that struck the entire U.S. electronics industry sapped INTERCON's strength until it became clear that it had outlived its usefulness. From all-time highs of 74 734 registrants and 1307 exhibitors in 1962, during the golden era of electronics growth in the United States, INTERCON began to slip. As late as 1969, 60 543 attendees and 618 exhibitors were reported by the convention managers, but only two years later the show's attendance had plunged to 35 228 and its exhibitors' list had shrunk enough for IEEE to announce a change in the convention management — from consultant to inhouse — but such cosmetic actions weren't the answer. By 1975, INTERCON's last year in existence, attendance was down to 20 471 — about one third of what it had been only six years before — and exhibitors were down to 190, less than 15 percent of what they had been in INTERCON's heyday.

Why would a manufacturer producing only MOS circuits suddenly decide to invest heavily in the relatively new bipolar technology of I<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>L? In General Instrument's case, the answer lies in the company's special interest in the consumer and telecommunications marketplaces. I<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>L promises to provide greater performance and reliability than existing LSI technologies, including n-channel MOS and CMOS.

High-performance linear and large-scale Schottky, TTL, and dense I<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>L functions on the same chip; innovative threshold and multilevel logic forms; 2000 I<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>L-gate custom bipolar arrays — these are but some of the ways in which I<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>L has reshaped standard functions and is creating next-generation integrated circuits.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: The insidious and cultural machine
abstract: It wasn't planned that way. Selden, Benz, Daimler, and Olds didn't envision it. Even Henry Ford, who, among them all, should have known, didn't. It took time to reveal the total impact of the automobile on society. In the beginning, misguided skeptics felt the more reliable horse, requiring only cheap and readily available fuels to charge his engines, would outlast the novelty of a noisy, smoke-belching gasoline-motor-driven carriage. But the gas buggy prevailed. And on its way to a position of dominance in today's economy, it left scarcely a facet of modern life untouched. That it all took place in so short a time span is attested to by the fact that there are those of us who remember the “tin lizzy” as it chugged from the showroom floor. Our children may never witness the sight and sound of a “flivver” laboring along a dusty country road, but our fathers surely did.

articleTitle: Electric energy: A global summary: The chairman of its program commission reports on major trends discussed at the recent World Electrotechnical Congress
abstract: As electric energy assumes ever-increasing importance in today's world, R&D efforts in electric power engineering have been intensifying to meet the need. In June, delegates from 42 nations met at the World Electrotechnical Congress in Moscow to review and discuss outstanding developments and trends in this field.

articleTitle: The automobile: For better or worse: Amid controversy about size, fuel consumption, and safety hazards, there is unanimity concerning the application of electronics to autos
abstract: Cadillac's chief engineer, Robert Templin, is hardly alone among his colleagues in the industry when he asks: “How much pollution is too much? How much fuel efficiency is enough? Who will pick up the tab for a zero-risk, zero-pollution car?” Never in its history has Detroit been faced with so many problems. Henry Ford himself might have opted for horse-drawn buggies instead of horseless carriages in the same situation.

Steps required include the extensive application of integrated electronic circuits for engine control The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) mobile source air pollution control program has one main objective — to protect health. The Clean Air Act charges the EPA with establishing and enforcing emission standards for automobiles to control emissions that cause or contribute to air pollution, which endangers the public welfare, as well as the public health. However, public welfare (or protection against economic losses caused by air pollution) is necessarily a secondary goal. The United States is so far from achieving the levels of clean air needed to protect health that it will not be meaningful to talk about emission control to protect welfare for some years to come.

articleTitle: Computer control of combined-cycle power plants: Complete automation and coordination of the plant is possible — From startup through loading, and from full load to shutdown
abstract: Combined-cycle power plants using gas-turbine and steam-turbine technology have a number of features that make them attractive to the electric utility industry — including low capital investment per kilowatt of generation; low daily operational costs; and capability for use as a base-load unit as well as a peaking station, with very fast start capabilities. And there is increasing interest in future use of low-energy gas from coal for combined-cycle power plants. Since this gas is clean burning, some air pollution problems can be avoided compared with power plants dependent on coal-fired steam generation by itself.

articleTitle: Consumer electronics: Single-slice superhet: New portable and table model AM/FM radios are designed with most active components on one 16-pin bipolar chip
abstract: Marketing a successful consumer product is essentially a story of cost control providing price advantage at retail. Electronic devices are no exception, assuming that the competitive edge is obtained without sacrificing those performance standards experienced customers have come to expect. It's a sobering thought, especially for engineers whose appreciation of things technical tends to equate product acceptance with improved quality.

articleTitle: Computers in Japan: Super coordination: Together, designers, equipment manufacturers, and the government spur progress
abstract: Japanese computer development, at least for larger systems, is a well-coordinated, highly organized effort. The Japanese Government considers computers strategic national products and so has guided domestic computer manufacturers into avenues of R&D designed to produce hardware, software, peripherals, and applications that will not only meet the needs of the dynamic Japanese economy, but will be effective state-of-the-art products, both in domestic and export markets. A key step to more effective competition was the Government decision, implemented during the early 1970s, to guide the six major Japanese computer manufacturers into forming three company groups dedicated to developing new and better computer systems.

articleTitle: Power generation: Constraints, yet progress: Technology helps power engineers circumvent problems: Land availability and population density
abstract: Japan ranks third in the world in electric power consumption, following the U.S. and the Soviet Union, with projections showing an average increase of 6.8 percent a year (Table I). Some 24.5 percent of this power is generated by hydroelectric stations, with fossil-fuel and nuclear generating plants accounting for 68 and 7.5 percent respectively. Advanced technologies help the Japanese power industry cope with the severe constraints of limited land availability and high population density.

articleTitle: Safety: The view from NHTSA: New legislation promises to make cars safer, cheaper to repair, and less polluting during the 1980s
abstract: Long a popular surrogate for sex, status, and derring-do, the American automobile is now adapting — rather abruptly — to rising energy costs and tough safety legislation. Manufacturers and motorists reluctantly realize that ego trips must be sacrificed to insure that essential commuting, shopping, and business excursions can continue in relative profusion and safety. Two major decisions announced by U.S. Secretary of Transportation Brock Adams during June 1977 have established a timetable for improved automobile crashworthiness and reduced operating cost.

The depressed economic situation afflicting the utilities in 1974-75 eased considerably in 1976, as the power industry achieved a more favorable stock equity and cash flow. Profit margins were up and the Dow-Jones utility average reflected a steady growth pattern. Thus, despite some dramatic incidents early in the year, such as the denunciation of the safety features in nuclear plants by three General Electric Company engineers and a licensing engineer with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (see Spectrum features on nuclear safety, May 1976), the industry fared quite well.

articleTitle: Aerospace: Conversations with a space shuttle Keeping experimenters in touch with orbiter-launched payloads requires a new earth-based communications support system
abstract: In less than three years, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's (NASA) space shuttle will become fully operational, ushering in a new era of orbital and interplanetary experiments. Important milestones involving hardware construction have already been passed. On September 17, 1976, the first of three (or possibly four) reusable space shuttle vehicles was rolled out for public display at Rockwell International's assembly plant in Palmdale, Calif. Officially called “Orbiter 101,” the spacecraft was soon christened the “Enterprise” by President Ford. (NASA spokesmen explain that fans of the television series “Star Trek” conducted a massive letter-writing campaign to the White House suggesting that the first space shuttle be named after the show's galaxy-hopping starship.)

articleTitle: Instrumentation: More bang for the buck: Test gear exploits complex integrated circuits to do more, faster
abstract: As a new year begins, the increasing use of large-scale integrated circuits (LSIs) by measurement-instrument manufacturers continues to increase instrument dollar value. At one end of the price scale, very-low-priced general-purpose instruments are proliferating and finding new applications in consumer and industrial markets, as a result of the availability of low-cost LSI chips. At the other end of the scale, sophisticated, higher-priced instruments — logic and microprocessor analyzers and microwave frequency counters and sources in the tens-of-gigahertz range — are being created to tackle complex circuit-design problems. And in between, traditional instruments such as digital multimeters are being upgraded by improving their performance (e.g., faster reading rates) and by adding capabilities, including the measurement of temperature, capacitance, and in-circuit semiconductor junction resistance.

articleTitle: The consumer and the automobile: Auto buyers don't always choose what's best for them, nor do makers always “read” consumers accurately
abstract: The U.S. automotive industry may be embarked on its most exciting era since its pioneering days, but not at the behest of the consumer. Pressed by the exigencies of the unfolding energy crisis and by legislative fiat, the automotive industry is developing new generations of vehicles that might best be described as “engineers' cars” — efficient automobiles that are by some standards in better taste and more value for the money. However reasonable this outcome may sound, it was arrived at in a way that flies in the face of the historic relationship of the industry to the market, a relationship in which, by a series of complicated, long-developed soundings, sensings, checks, and balances, the industry produces what the consumer indicates he wants. That is not the same as what he may accept, and the difference is a very significant one for many reasons, all of them serious.

In rail transportation, European manufacturers are having considerable success in selling their products in the United States -and this appears to be an accelerating trend. Take Amtrak, the quasi-Governmental U.S. corporation that operates most intercity passenger trains. This transportation giant is investing a billion dollars in Federal funds in French and Swedish traction equipment - and for track and roadbed improvements - rather than in equipment from U.S. companies. Why? The answer is that, in the early 1970s, when Amtrak started its search for a new type of high-speed train, none was available from domestic builders. In fact, consumer use of air routes in the U.S. had come to dominate rail travel to such a degree that U.S. locomotive builders either went out of business or concentrated their efforts on producing large, freight-hauling traction machines. Consequently, the door was opened to Swedish, French, Swiss, and Italian suppliers who are queuing up for an even larger share of the U.S. rail transportation pie - both in urban mass-transit and main-line routes.

articleTitle: Automotive electronics: Betting on the future: Dramatic experiments may help improve the already bright outlook for the Japanese automotive industry
abstract: Like their colleagues in other countries, Japanese automobile manufacturers have been making steady strides in the introduction of electronics to the automobile. Such devices and/or systems as electronic ignition, fuel injection, windshield-wiper control, and climate control are available either as standard or optional equipment on Japanese automobiles. In addition, because the country's exhaust-emission standards are the toughest in the world, the Japanese have focused considerable research and development on emission control.

From the point of view of EFT protagonists, progress is being made on all fronts. In the regulatory area, for example, some 26 states have passed enabling legislation that makes possible the installation of essentially all types of EFT equipment and defines the conditions under which installations can be made. In general, the effect of such legislation is either to remove the concept that an EFT terminal must be considered a branch or to make the branching requirement for installing most EFT equipment extremely modest.

articleTitle: Tougher jobs, tougher instruments: More complex measurement problems are being solved by microprocessors, bussed systems, and software
abstract: Electronic test and measurement instruments have been changing dramatically as the basic technologies from which they spring have become more complex, and the problems they must solve more difficult. Today's instruments are being designed to span broader ranges of frequency and amplitude than ever before, and with greater precision. At the same time, instruments are expected to offer improved speed and convenience so that design, production, and maintenance tests can be accomplished more quickly and more efficiently. Users require, and expect, greatly enhanced capabilities from instruments that continue to operate at high levels of reliability.
Describes the development of instrument rental industry. Once an army/navy store operation, the instrument rental industry is respectable and thriving, and discusses why and what it can offer.

articleTitle: Career management: Taxes and the second income: For the U.S. engineer: Experts tell how to ease the tax bite on your alternate income
abstract: Moonlighting — with a second job or self-employment — can increase an engineer's income, but it can also increase tax payments. That's why knowledge of current tax requirements and practices can help the engineer protect the benefits a second income promises to provide. Those who work for more than one employer should be particularly aware of the tax consequences of excess Social Security tax payments and of the deductions that can be made for commutation expenses between jobs.

I<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>L or, more simply, injection logic, presents significant advantages over n-channel MOS technology in two major areas: products that must operate at high speeds and applications that require analog and digital functions to be combined on the same chip. Seeking to exploit the potential advantages fully, Fairchild has applied dielectric-isolation techniques to I<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>L and come up with a speed-and density-enhancing version called Isoplanar integrated-injection logic, or I<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>L®.

In the important area of high-speed digital LSI circuits, I<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>L represents a higher-density complement to low-power Schottky-TTL technology. Functions requiring a circuit complexity of 500 gates or less probably could be produced economically by use of a standard low-power Schottky process. But for greater-complexity chips that operate over −55 to +125°C, I<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>L is needed.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: The age of the survey
abstract: “The American People appear to be losing confidence in President Carter's ability to restore trust in government, according to the latest quarterly New York Times/CBS News poll,” the Times reported on its front page recently. The ultimate implications resident in this and other outputs of the quarterly poll were left largely to the reader. Franklin Roosevelt, Harry Truman, and even Dwight Eisenhower had neither the benefits nor the disadvantages of frequent polls like these. Such surveys, and others like them, test today's political leaders' sagacity and intestinal fortitude in exploiting or surviving them.

articleTitle: The automobile: It's the super-driver of both technology and society
abstract: Automotive developments have played a major positive role in the civilization of the 20th century. Two important elements of a successful and expanding economy are transportation and industrialization. In this regard, the automobile has. on balance, provided man with infinitely more advantages than disadvantages. With the help of automotive technology, for example, a man can plow over 100 acres in an eight-hour day. With a team of oxen, that same man in the same amount of time could plow less than an acre.

articleTitle: Automotive electronics I: Smaller and better: Electronics may be the only cost-effective solution to the performance challenge of today's autos
abstract: The applications of electronics in today's automobiles, and those of tomorrow, are gaining momentum rapidly. This increase can be attributed to many factors — the increased density, lower cost, and improved reliability of solid-state devices as a result of LSI technology; a closer working relationship between automotive and electronics manufacturers; the need to meet ever more stringent Government regulations for fuel economy and exhaust emissions; and the automotive industry's desire to provide customers with a wide selection of subsystems with practical benefits that are cost-effective.

articleTitle: Closed-loop engine control: Analog or digital circuits to aid emissions control may be the forerunner of onboard engine “tuning”
abstract: To meet current U.S. emissions standards for automobiles, hydrocarbon (HC) and carbon monoxide (CO) emissions are usually controlled by a catalytic converter in the automobile exhaust. Federal standards for nitrogen oxides (NO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">x</inf>) emissions are met mainly by exhaust-gas recirculation (EGR) techniques. However, in 1981, when NO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">x</inf> emissions standards are tightened from the current limit of 2.0 grams per mile to 1.0 gram per mile, these techniques alone may no longer be sufficient.

articleTitle: Inventing the negative feedback amplifier: Six years of persistent search helped the author conceive the idea “in a flash” aboard the old Lackawanna Ferry
abstract: Recently, while watching television at my home in New Jersey, I was pleasantly surprised to see a commercial for a computer-controlled sewing machine. It was the latest of many applications of the negative feedback amplifier that I could never have envisioned when I invented the amplifier more than 50 years ago as a 29-year-old systems engineer at the Western Electric Company's old West Street laboratories in New York City. Although I was certain the amplifier would see broad use inside as well as outside of the Bell System, I did not foresee the tremendous range of applications that would open up for it in almost every type of communication and control system, from radio to automatic pilots, from computers to artificial limbs. The enormous impact of what I had conceived while traveling to work one sunny August morning in 1927 has proved extremely gratifying. I am proud that the amplifier is used today in more than 85 countries and that it has played such an important role in the technological revolution of the past half-century.

articleTitle: Graphics displays: Users are enticed by decreasing hardware costs and greater availability of software
abstract: Computer-aided graphics-display systems once were regarded as something of a cure in search of a disease. Though they easily fulfilled the old adage that a single picture — in this case, one generated or enhanced by computer — is worth a thousand words, efforts at practical applications were thwarted by limited software and by prohibitively high equipment costs.

articleTitle: Semiconductors face the '80s: Seven leaders of the boomingest business in the U.S. prognosticate the problems supergrowth could lead to
abstract: Gordon Moore, president of Intel, put it succinctly: “By 1986, the semiconductor industry could be producing something of the order of 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">14</sup> functions per year. Who will use it all?” He, and 800 other participants in a recent colloquium in California's Silicon Valley, organized by the Santa Clara Chapter of IEEE's Electron Devices Society, heard some attempts at answers from industry leaders. But Dr. Moore was not satisfied. The rate of growth is such, he told Spectrum in a follow-up interview, that if the industry stays on its present upward curve of producing functions and tries to solve its problems as it always has in the past — by lowering prices — there will come a time in the 1980s when it could face disruption and a significant drop in revenues. “And that,” he says, “despite exciting new markets on the horizon, in an otherwise blossoming economy, could be a disaster.”

articleTitle: Telecommunications: Meeting through your computer: Information exchange and engineering decision-making are made easy through computer-assisted conferencing
abstract: As you read this article, 15 scientists from the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) and three Energy Research and Development Administration (ERDA) National Laboratories are meeting to discuss modeling the impact on several western states of strip and underground mining, new power plants, and other schemes for energy extraction. At another meeting, several administrators from USGS offices in Menlo Park, Calif., and Reston, Va., are evaluating a contract proposal. At a third meeting, econometricians and other specialists are exploring the problems associated with the various approaches to modeling the U.S. economy.

articleTitle: Communications: Optical transmission of voice and data: Bandwidth and noise immunity are up; size, weight, and costs are down
abstract: Fiber-optic transmission systems offer powerful advantages over conventional coaxial cable and metallic wire links. Increased bandwidth, smaller diameter, lower weight, lack of crosstalk, complete immunity to inductive interference, and the potential ability to deliver signals at lower costs are bringing fiber-optic systems out of the laboratory into strong competition with conventional systems in telecommunications, computers, military systems, and many other areas.

articleTitle: The pervasive microprocessor: Trends and prospects: The progressive EE cannot afford to overlook new microprocessor technologies and applications. The author, an expert, tells why
abstract: As microprocessors diffuse into a myriad of applications in factories and offices, and in the automobiles and homes of ordinary citizens, semiconductors and the related industries that spawned these processors-on-a-chip have been undergoing profound changes. Requirements for the great circuit complexity called for in microcomputer-system elements — processors, memories, and input-output circuits — have been met by a flowering of semiconductor technologies, among which the metal-oxide semiconductor (MOS) is outdistancing all competitors. These technologies are expected to offer a million devices per chip by the early 1980s, a complexity level that challenges the imagination of system designers.

articleTitle: Nuclear fusion: Focus on Tokamak: U.S. engineers and physicists will team to attempt commercial demonstration by the year 2000
abstract: Prospects for generation of electric power from controlled nuclear fusion — the harnessing of energy released during the combination of very light atomic nuclei to form somewhat heavier ones — are meeting with renewed enthusiasm, as a result of significant progress in this area since 1968. Nevertheless, the technology still is far from commercial reality, whereas the use of controlled nuclear fission — involving energy released in the splitting of very heavy atomic nuclei into lighter ones — has been accepted commercially for some time. For example, in the U.S., the goal for a practical demonstration of fusion energy is the end of the century. In the meantime, the emphasis in the nation's fusion program has been shifting from research to engineering and technology.

articleTitle: Solid state: Synonym for progress: For Japan, semiconductor technology is where electronics really began, and where it is going
abstract: Japanese electronics manufacturers are making major efforts in the development of advanced semiconductor integrated-circuit (IC) products. Long considered adept at copying designs of others, they are now producing innovative digital IC designs of their own.

articleTitle: Lessons from ‘Project Whirlwind’: A talented team produced many computer “firsts,” and added new chapters to R&D management texts
abstract: New technical and scientific perceptions often evoke practical engineering and management techniques that ultimately force the state of the art. Such was the impact in 1945 of the then new and revolutionary concept of the electronic digital computer upon a group of brash young engineers (as they so struck their elders), who proceeded to build a computer of maverick, pioneer design on the campus of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. The computer was named “Whirlwind” by its Navy sponsors even before they knew how fast it would really be. Its design and construction were directed by Jay W. Forrester, inventor of magnetic-core storage, and Robert R. Everett, whose unique computer “block diagrams” would soon be showing a generation of engineers how to undertake the design of computers.

articleTitle: Microprocessors: Microprocessors talk it up: Micros, alone and in constellations, are star feature of new radio, telephone, data, and satellite systems
abstract: Whether it is a mobile radio, telephone, data, or satellite communication system, if it was developed during the past year or two, it probably includes at least one micro-computer. As the micro takes over one area of communications after another, the idea that computers-on-a-chip are replacements for hard-wired logic is being replaced by the realization that the micro introduces intelligence. Micros are magnificient in those communications applications where data bits are handled, at the system interfaces where human beings interact, and in communications control and switching functions. Right now, it seems they are too slow to handle hard-core communications tasks such as filtering, but for coding, formatting, displaying, monitoring, multiplexing, queuing, and microsecond-to-microsecond management of communications, the micros are proving a valuable resource.

articleTitle: Power: Planning for a brighter future: Modeling and simulation, load forecasting, frequency control, stability, security, and reliability are important factors
abstract: Ever since the Mideast oil embargo of 1973-74, the electric utilities of the world's industrial nations have been confronted by the aggravating necessity of coping with unprecedented “power plays” and “power ploys” as rising costs of fossil fuels, labor, transportation, materials, and construction heralded the irreversible transition from cheap energy to increasingly expensive power production. The initial effect of this abrupt change was surprise: Plans that were projected over the course of the next decade, and beyond, had to be revised as designs went back to the drawing boards.

articleTitle: State of the audiotape art: Amateurs and professionals find their favorite tape formats enhanced by better electronics, mechanics, and magnetic oxides
abstract: Short-wave radio listeners eavesdropping on German broadcasts during World War II were among the first to realize that audio recording technology had entered a new era. Somehow “live” orchestra performances were emanating from occupied Europe on a time schedule unrelated to the musicians' logistics problems or sleeping habits. When hostilities ended, the secret was revealed — a new electronic marvel called the Magnetophon that recorded almost flawlessly on reels of iron-oxide-impregnated tape. Gone were the hiss, crackle, and miserable frequency response long associated with disc, sound on film, and wire recording techniques.

articleTitle: Solid-state devices: The traditional bipolar vs. MOS battle lines are blurring
abstract: The past year saw established bipolar and metal-oxide semiconductor (MOS) technologies stretched to their limits to produce the densest, most complex integrated circuits yet. However, that very effort suggested the time might be at hand to exploit the potential of a new generation of technologies waiting in the wings. Bipolar integrated-injection logic (I2L), MOS-based charge-coupled devices (CCDs), and even solid-state bubble devices, among others, all seemed ready to meet at least some of the challenges.

articleTitle: Magnetic tape: A high performer: Magnetic tape has evolved into a highly effective medium for high-density and low-cost-per-bit data recording
abstract: Low cost is the underlying reason for the continued popularity of magnetic tape. Still the least expensive recording medium available for applications such as instrumentation, its present per-bit price range of 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−4</sup>–10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−6</sup> cents (for access times ranging from 10 ms to 100 seconds) — coupled with the high recording densities the tape is capable of providing — also makes it an extremely attractive and practical storage medium. However, although today's magnetic tape for analog- and digital-signal storage may look much the same, and work on the same principle, as its earliest predecessor did some 40 years ago, steady and important improvements have been realized in its performance.

articleTitle: ATE: Not so easy: As components and subsystems become more complex, automatic testing grows difficult and costly
abstract: The demands of production-line testing pose both challenge and frustration to designers of automatic test equipment (ATE). The challenge is to continually enhance the capabilities of the equipment so that system designers, ever on the alert to utilize the latest components, will be able to maintain high production throughput. The frustration is that each important technology advance in integrated circuits has made the job of automatic testing an increasingly difficult — if not impossible — and costly one to accomplish.

articleTitle: Independent test labs: Caveat emptor: Although this industry is nearly 15 years old, is growing rapidly, and performs a needed service, it remains fraught with controversy
abstract: “Burn-in? Hardly anyone, anywhere, Is performing It properly.”

articleTitle: Semiconductors: Toeing the (microfine) line: Functional density is what counts in advanced solid-state devices. Here's a report on recent progress
abstract: The maturing of processing equipment, the development of new processes, and the wide exploitation of existing dimensional capabilities — all these are pushing LSI IC functional densities to new heights. And in the forefront of this push are efforts to improve the resolution of IC photolithographic and other fabrication techniques.

articleTitle: Automotive electronics II: The microprocessor is in: This tiny IC will satisfy the government's requirements for energy and pollution control as well as the consumer's preference for luxury
abstract: Caught between conflicting Government regulations and consumer demands, automobile manufacturers are investigating the use of microprocessor integrated circuits (ICs) as sophisticated control elements to bridge these seemingly irreconcilable differences.

articleTitle: Communications satellites: Looking to the 1980s: It will be a decade of new and exciting applications, lower costs, and more reliable service
abstract: How will satellite communications evolve in the decade 1980–1990? In answer to that question, some prognostications appear reasonably certain of fulfillment: • The INTELSAT global communications system will continue to grow, providing existing services at lower cost and introducing new services. • Domestic and regional systems will continue to expand. • The Space Transportation System will have a major impact. • Technological advances will allow systems with complexity and capability probably an order of magnitude greater than present-day systems. • Applications will expand from classical point-to-point telephony and broadcast into many new areas.

articleTitle: Toward safer motor vehicles: Many “fatal” accidents can be survived, or avoided altogether, by adopting vehicle designs that stress safety over styling
abstract: No value is greater than that we set on human life, and so, to those concerned with the automobile, no responsibility is more important than the safety of passengers, drivers, transportation workers, and pedestrians. Yet you and I are the primary cause of needless highway accidents, not just because we impact roadside objects, pedestrians, and each other, but also because we tolerate safety deficiencies in our vehicles and in the highway system. It is time to demand reasonable action, to identify major safety problems, and to find and implement the most effective solutions. The lives saved and suffering prevented, combined with the economic savings involved, more than justify the research efforts and the cost of implementing them.

While PAC members still voice complaints with regard to USAB's program, there was nothing but praise for USAB Vice President John Guarrera's handling of a free-wheeling, three-day PAC workshop held at the end of March in Arlington, Va. The advertised purpose of the workshop, the second USAB has sponsored in six months, was to sample “grass roots” sentiment on professional issues, as well as to open the doors to two-way communication. If Arlington is any barometer of success, than USAB rates a gold star when it comes to communication. At Arlington, the wires were burning up.

articleTitle: Consumer electronics: everybody's doing it (`computing' at home): the demand for owner-operated microcomputers has blossomed, creating a brand-new market for kits, peripherals, and software
abstract: Slavery is immoral, servants are expensive, and socio-political consciousness raising has given the family pet a monopoly on loyalty and obedience. Yet the human ego still longs to dominate a more productive, skilled, and responsible entity.

IEEE General Manager and Executive Director H. A. Schulke, Jr., has tendered his resignation effective July 22, 1977. In a letter to 1977 IEEE President Robert Saunders, Dr. Schulke cited as his reason for leaving “the burgeoning scope of USAB programs into new areas of activity and the amount of time and effort required to be spent in determining what the extent of these activities should be.” Said Dr. Schulke in his letter to Dr. Saunders, “In attempting to meet USAB's demands, I do not find the time to address properly the many other important activities of the Institute or to engage in technical activities. For me, such technical activity is an essential element of professional satisfaction and one that I hoped I would find as IEEE's General Manager. Such is not the case though.”

articleTitle: Power/energy: Nontraditional sources: A sampler: Engineers in Israel, France, and the U.K. choose their own ways to go in the energy crisis
abstract: In view of the energy shortage in so many parts of the world, unconventional sources of power are being studied in a number of countries. However, the approach can scarcely be considered unified and each nation has its own priorities. To obtain a sampling of some typical activities in this area for Spectrum, in September 1976 I visited three countries with markedly different energy situations — Israel, France, and the United Kingdom. Among the contrasts: Israel has no conventional fossil fuels and France has hardly any, while Great Britain, beginning in 1979, is expected to have a surplus of oil and gas that should last 15 to 20 years, as well as a substantial coal reserve — which should provide the British with adequate “breathing space” in which to develop the so-called alternative energy sources. Unlike Israel, both France and Britain have advanced commercial nuclear power technology (see “Europe: tilting toward fusion” in Spectrum, Dec. 1976, p. 37) while Israel has an abundance of solar radiation not shared by parts of France and most of the United Kingdom.

articleTitle: ‘What ifs?’ for nuclear plants: Sophisticated reliability analyses and risk assessments are aimed at predicting failures and their consequences
abstract: Hundreds of thousands of electrical and electronic components are imbedded in the systems that operate and monitor a typical nuclear power generating station. To predict the reliability of systems containing these components and the risks involved in operating these stations, the nuclear power industry is slowly but surely accepting reliability analysis. Using these techniques, the analyst systematically challenges the design by asking a series of “what if” questions, concerning potential component failures, always probing for design weaknesses. Many utilities are now employing such methods in reliability analyses directed to improving the availability of their power-generating facilities and thus increasing the energy output obtained for each dollar invested in these facilities. Using qualitative and, more recently, quantitative techniques, reliability analysis is gradually becoming a regular, day-to-day tool of nuclear power plant design.

articleTitle: Engine options for the car of tomorrow: Competing internal and external combustion engines, as well as electrics, are considered as contenders
abstract: Predicting what engine will power tomorrow's cars goes far beyond the technical feasibility of meeting emissions and fuel-economy requirements. Such forecasting encompasses the traditional pressures of competition, cost, and consumer acceptance — as well as performance, durability, and serviceability, along with requirements for training and parts supply. Uncertainty as to the type of fuel available is another complicating factor. R&D costs and the availability of capital for tools and facilities are also considerations.

articleTitle: Managing the creative engineer: A probe into the characteristics of the creative engineer, the sensitive manager, and the favorable environment
abstract: Few subjects in the management literature have produced as much abstruse verbiage as the question of how best to deal with creative people.
