In an effort to glean some concrete insights that would be relevant to managers of electrical engineers, Spectrum organized an ELECTRO '77 panel discussion on the topic of identifying, stimulating, and nurturing creative technical professionals. The following is a condensation of remarks made during that session as well as during preliminary meetings between the panelists and Spectrum.

abstract: In an unusually substantive two-day meeting on February 19-20, in Washington, D.C., IEEE's Board of Directors took several actions that could have major consequences for the Institute in the near future. articleTitle: Power/energy: UHV: Onward and upward: A major effort is being mounted in the U.S. and overseas to push practical transmission above the 1000-kV level
abstract: Transmission systems, with special emphasis on ultrahigh voltage (1000 kV and higher), presently constitute a top-priority technology R&D effort both in the United States and overseas. One of the reasons for the accelerated international push in UHV over the past three years may be the result of the 1973-74 Mideast oil embargo. The subsequent energy crisis heightened an awareness of the need for more efficient energy utilization in the generation and transmission of electricity — especially to load centers remote from sources of generation. Specifically, UHV transmission efficiency is greater than that of EHV, and line losses are less. And it is hoped that the increased cost of UHV overhead line construction and rights-of-way acquisition will be more than offset by the larger transmission capacity.

articleTitle: Constraining the energy gobbler: Industry is the principal energy consumer; technology exists to save fuel and, of course, dollars
abstract: That U.S. industry has been selected as the prime target for energy conservation is not mere chance. As the largest energy-consuming sector in the nation, industry gulps some 40 percent of the total fuel used each year. However, it is estimated that up to about 20 percent of that amount could be saved through the use of innovative technologies (Fig. 1) that should result in dollar as well as fuel economies.

A solid-state conversion terminal is the heart of a new “coal by wire” power project that moves energy 734 km (456 mi) between Center, N. Dak., and Duluth, Minn. The ac power generated by the Square Butte Electric Cooperative, near the lignite fields of Center, is converted to direct current and sent via dc transmission line for use by the Minnesota Power and Light Company of Duluth. The dc transmission line is rated at ±250 kV, 1000 amperes. At Duluth, the dc energy is reconverted into ac power for use by the utility's customers. The system was built by the General Electric Company. By contrast, one proposed ac tie line between the two sites would have required more than twice the right-of-way cable miles as compared with that for the dc line as well as much wider right-of-ways to accommodate the greater number of conductors and wires needed for ac transmission.

Computer readout systems are the heart of new laser printers introduced recently by the Xerox Corporation and the Eastman Kodak Company, Both systems offer the advantage of being able to store the information necessary to print business forms or other material so that inventories of such forms are not necessary. The Xerox 9700 electronic printing system uses standard 8½- by 11-inch paper and prints two pages a second, up to 18 000 lines per minute, depending on type size and format. Operating from magnetic tape or directly from a computer, the system creates images electronically and utilizes a laser scanner to project images of both the form being used and its contents for simultaneous printing. To be available in the third quarter of 1978, a basic system will rent for $5300 a month on a one-year lease or may be purchased for $295 000, The Kodak system takes computer information and deposits it on 16-mm microfilm or 105-mm microfiche film rolls, which are processed dry by being passed over a heated drum for 5 seconds. A laser is used to expose the film. The Komstar 300 sells for $143 225 and will be marketed this year in selected U.S. cities, with nationwide distribution in 1978.

abstract: This column will comment at random on a commodity most of us used to take for granted, and one that some of us still do: water. To be available in the U.S. in the Spring of 1978, the Konica C35AF compact 35 mm camera will offer an electronic automatic focusing system in addition to automatic exposure and automatic built-in flash. The camera incorporates Honeywell's Visitronic Auto/Focus module, an IC 2.5 by 6 mm with two light-sensitive detector areas. It compares an image falling on one of the detectors with an image falling on the other. When the two images generate maximum correlation (maximum output voltage from the IC), the IC prouces a step-function voltage change which works with external control ciruitry to automatically position the lens in the camera. The camera is the product of Konishiroku Photo Industry Co., Ltd. of Tokyo, Japan, and will be marketed in the U.S. by Konica Camera Company.

Solar cells that combine liquids and solids show promise for important advantages compared with all-solid cells. According to Bell Labs, developer of the liquid-junction cells, the devices are more economical than all-solid cells because they use less expensive polycrystalline materials and are more economical to make. The new cells have two electrodes immersed in a water-based solution. One of the electrodes is a semiconducting material; the other can be made of carbon or a variety of common metals. When light falls on the semiconductor, current flows from one electrode to the other via the liquid. With the polycrystalline form of cadmium selenide as the semiconductor electrode, Bell Labs has found that 5.1 percent of the light is converted to electricity. The more expensive single-crystal form of cadmium selenide gives a conversion efficiency of 7.5 percent. Chemicals in the solution for the liquid/solid cells are affected little by the conversion process. A three- to four-year life has been simulated.

Using an advanced ion-implanted, high-density metal-gate complementary MOS process, the National Semiconductor Corporation, Santa Clara, Calif., has produced, on a single 28 000-square-mil chip, a true 8-bit analog-to-digital converter with latched outputs, a 16-channel expandable multiplexer with address input latches, provision for handling external signal conditioning, and all the logic control needed for interfacing the chip to all standard microcomputers. The new +5-volt single-supply device, the ADC0816 (MM74C948), is priced at $19.95 in quantities of 100 and is said to replace $100 to $200 worth of hybrid and discrete component analog boards. The 40-pin unit performs a conversion in 50 microseconds. At 25°C, linearity, zero error, and full-scale error are no more than ±½ least significant bit each. The chip is suitable for application in medical instruments, process control, industrial control, and machine control.

A National Project on Philosophy and Engineering Ethics will pair engineers and philosophers to develop and implement joint projects in engineering ethics — including research on specific ethical problems and case studies, teaching projects, and projects in conjunction with professional engineering societies. Phase 1 of the three-phase project — which has been funded by the National Endowment for the Humanities and will be administered through the Center for the Study of the Human Dimensions of Science and Technology at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute — includes an Institute on Philosophical Ethics for Engineers, an Institute for Philosophers on Ethical Problems in Engineering, and a joint workshop on Projects in Engineering Ethics. The events will be held on the R.P.I. campus in Troy, N.Y., July 16–August 5, 1978. Phase 2, scheduled for the 1978–79 academic year, will have each team work out the details of its project, which is to be completed during the 1979–80 academic year.

Following hot on the heels of the widely touted CAT scanners using X-ray transmissions are the new ECAT (Emission Computerized Axial Tomographic) scanners. Instead of computer-constructed images dependent upon X-ray transmissions through the head or body, ECAT scanners give computer-constructed images based upon concentrations of radiopharmaceuticals administered to a patient and distributed throughout the body according to known physiological phenomena. The images represent the metabolic activity occurring within a “slice” through the patient and can aid a physician in the diagnosis and treatment of malignancies, heart attacks, strokes, and other body ailments.

articleTitle: Feedback from IEEE's long-range planning report: While the report may have largely failed as a blueprint for change, it has confirmed the Institute's need for advance planning
abstract: “Long Range Plans,” an ambitious report written by IEEE's Long Range Planning Committee over a three-year period from 1973 to 1975 and described in last month's Spectrum (p. 60), has been under attack ever since its release a little more than a year ago. abstract: The following article was commissioned by Spectrum following the potentially momentous action of IEEE's Board of Directors at its February meeting calling for, among other things, the abolishment of the industrial exemption. The purpose of this article is to provide IEEE members with some of the key facts regarding the status of registration today — uncolored by bias for or against the Board action. articleTitle: The IEEE as a ‘black box’ Five members — Ranging in both experience and philosophy — Face off in a discussion of where we are and ought to be
abstract: On April 22, during ELECTRO'77 in New York City, Spectrum gathered five IEEE members together for the purpose of airing conflicting views on the state of the Institute. Chosen for this informed colloquium were EEs with no political ax to grind — that is, none had evinced any intention to run for IEEE office and so had no constituency to whom he or she might be beholden. On the other hand, each had expressed great concern for the fate of the Institute over the years — via activity on a national or local level and via letters to Spectrum. The result was an all-day debate that exposed many of the most profound divisions within the IEEE membership at large. What follows is a summary of opinions voiced — on IEEE's technical activities, on its professional activities, and on the EE as a professional interacting with society. As might be expected in any discussion of complex issues, no conclusions were reached, nor will they be drawn by Spectrum; rather, they are left to the reader.

Reflecting increased newspaper employment advertising, the Deutsch, Shea, and Evans demand index for engineers and scientists hit 139.8 in April, up from a March figure of 120.5. However, while DS&E's subindex data for April show that both classified and display newspaper advertising increased strongly, technical journal employment advertising declined. DS&E believes further demand index gains are likely over the next few months, explaining that lead time and other factors cause recruiting programs in technical journals to lag those conducted via newspaper. DS&E index figures are derived directly from monthly totals of employment listings in key newspapers and technical journals.

Richard Aseltine has joined IEEE's Field Services staff in New York as Manager, Student Services. In this capacity, he is responsible for all aspects of programs and services for the Institute's 25 000 Student members in 440 Student Branches at educational institutions throughout the world.

The models MDAS-16 and MDAS-8 are the industry's first 12-bit data-acquisition systems fabricated with thin-film hybrid technology, according to the manufacturer. The devices incorporate a CMOS multiplexer; a programmable gain instrumentation amplifier; a sample-hold, 10-volt buffered reference; a 12-bit A/D converter; an address register; and the digital control logic into a 62-pin package that measures 5.84 by 3.56 by 0.61 cm.

One of the first steps that James Schlesinger will take in his role as Secretary of the newly created U.S. Department of Energy will be to address Federal energy research functions, which previously resided in the U.S. Energy Research and Development Administration. Under the reorganization act, these functions will be reassigned to one or more of eight new Assistant Secretaries. Dr. Schlesinger has indicated that he intends to streamline the research organization to make it more responsive to national needs.

The Continental Ballroom complex at the Hilton Hotel will be the site of 30 of WESCON's 32 professional sessions. In addition, two student sessions will be held at the TownHouse Hotel. Chairing the program is L. Terry Jackson of Lawrence Berkeley Laboratories; Alan B. Grebene, Exar Integrated Systems, is vice chairman. Sessions will be held at 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. daily throughout the meeting.

articleTitle: Special report: Convention new products at WESCON '77
abstract: Adding up to its largest “show” in San Francisco since 1969, WESCON '77's 400 exhibitors will be displaying a variety of electrical/electronic products in some 680 booths. On exhibit will be semiconductor devices such as memories, microprocessors, power devices and displays, instruments, production equipment, subsystem modules, and large systems for a variety of functions (automatic testing, control, etc.). A number of prominent semiconductor companies will be exhibiting, including RCA Semiconductor, Plessey Semiconductor, Advanced Micro Devices, and Mostek. Other well-known semiconductor manufacturers will show their wares through distributors at the show.

Four floating nuclear power plants have been ordered by the Public Service Electric and Gas Company of New Jersey, with the first unit scheduled for delivery in 1984. The plants will be produced by Offshore Power Systems, a wholly owned subsidiary of the Westinghouse Electric Corporation, at its Blount Island manufacturing facility — which is currently under construction near Jacksonville, Fla. According to Richard M. Eckert, vice president of engineering and construction at PSE&G, the floating plants offer a number of benefits, including reduced construction time, production-line efficiency due to standardization, factory pretesting, and siting flexibility.

Prospects that the Congress will move swiftly on President Carter's energy proposals are dim, with a number of different committees slated to participate in the legislative process. In the Senate, the Energy and Natural Resources Committee and the Finance Committee will have primary jurisdiction over the policy aspects of the proposed legislation, but five other committees also will have an opportunity to provide inputs. In the House, Speaker O'Neill has set up an Ad Hoc Committee on Energy to coordinate the work of the five standing committees that will share in reviewing the legislation.

articleTitle: Awards: The new fellows: IEEE's latest additions to its elite grade are named and the selection process is briefly described
abstract: Each year, the IEEE Board of Directors elevates a group of the Institute's Senior Members to the grade of Fellow. This election is a great honor because, according to the IEEE Bylaws, the Fellow grade is one of “unusual professional distinction, to be conferred upon a person of outstanding and extraordinary qualifications and experience in the fields of electrical engineering, electronics, radio, allied branches of engineering, or the related arts and sciences, who has made important individual contributions to one or more of these fields.” The key words in this definition of the Fellow grade are “outstanding” and “extraordinary.” According to the Bylaws, no more than 0.6 percent (revised upward in 1976 from 0.5 percent) of IEEE Senior Members may be elected Fellows in any one year; moreover, the annual number of elected Fellows may not exceed 0.1 percent of the Institute membership exclusive of Students and Associates. Translated, this means that, over the last decade, there had never been more than 127 Fellows elected in any one year until 1976, when the previously mentioned Bylaw revision permitted a maximum of 133 elections.

Field troubleshooting, to the component level, of microprocessor-based products designed with Hewlett-Packard's new signature-analysis service technique has been greatly simplified. Using the 5004A Signature Analyzer instrument, faulty bit streams can be located in microprocessor-based circuits with an accuracy of 99.998 percent.

Ivan A. Getting, president of the Aerospace Corporation, has been elected President of IEEE for 1978. Dr. Getting received 28 161 votes to defeat Irwin Feerst (21 753 votes) in the third contested election held by the Institute. The new Executive Vice President is C. Lester Hogan, who defeated Carleton A. Bayless for this office.

This ten-page note presents a theoretical basis for standards used in measuring the loss parameters of capacitors at 1 MHz. The problems of accurately measuring Q are explained, and equations are developed to describe measurement error and uncertainty, Use of conductance elements in this type of Q-measurement is discussed and various circuit arrangements that will allow accurate results are presented and explained. Desirable characteristics of standard capacitances are described.

This 12-page note explains the basic design concepts and theory of operation of instruments that measure microwave attenuation. The relative merits of series and parallel substitution systems are discussed, and operation of a parallel-type system is described. Elements of an attenuation calibrator systjm are described. These include the IF system, null indicating circuitry, reference generator, and AFC circuits. The significance of noise balance is explained.

Spokesmen for Zenith Radio Corporation, Glenview, Ill., say the company is making continuing efforts to relocate 600 salaried employees affected by a September 28 cutback, and has initiated programs to help sharpen interview-taking and résumé-writing skills. Of the salaried group affected, those with ten or more years' seniority will remain on the payroll until December 31, 1977. All others were terminated immediately and given severance pay based on length of service. Following months of financial difficulties and a mid-September reorganization of its engineering, research, and management activities, Zenith announced the layoffs as part of a sweeping cost-reduction program (see News from Industry in this issue, p. 115).

Wide-band transformer design and shielding attenuation are covered in ten pages of application notes. The transformer discussion begins with the requirements for these devices, then explains the lumped element equivalent circuit for wide-band transformers. Measurements of ferrite transformer materials are then covered. Alternative core shapes for these transformers are discussed, and the significance of form factor is explained.

The political struggle over the future of the Clinch River Fast Breeder Reactor Project has shown signs of intensifying with Edison Electric Institute president W. Donham Crawford's recent urging of the U.S. Congress to override Preident Carter's veto of the bill authorizing the project. The veto, according to Mr. Crawford, would foreclose the development of that source of energy in the United States as an option for the latter part of this century or the beginning of the next one.

Higher costs for electricity consumers in the U.S. are expected as a result of energy legislation recently adopted by the House of Representatives. This conclusion was made in a recent survey by the Edison Electric Institute (EEI). As an example, the oil tax would add $834 million to the operational costs of the Southern California Edison Company through 1988, and the cost of converting that company's generating facilities from oil to coal is estimated at $3 billion.

The Consolidated Edison Company will increase its generating capacity in operation in New York City as a precautionary measure in the event of a storm threat to any of the company's major installations. This is just one of a series of interim steps Con Ed has been taking to prevent another major blackout such as the one that occurred on the night of July 13. Other measures include such steps as the reduction of imported power into the company's service areas (resulting in increases in cost and pollution), increases in staff at Con Ed's energy control center and other installations, improvements in the “black start” capability of gas turbines, and the upgrading of telephone and radio communications. Meanwhile, an investigation of the recent blackout by the company's review board is underway, with a report to the public expected momentarily.

articleTitle: Medical diagnostics: Visual/aural techniques: High-resolution scanning systems, a retinal camera, and a cardiac-output earpiece show promise
abstract: One of the most active areas of biomedical engineering is ultrasonic diagnosis. In Japan, as in other parts of the world, developments in ultrasonic diagnostic equipment are fast paced. Interest in the technique is great because it is noninvasive, unlike many competing techniques, and because the potential for early diagnosis of certain body malfunctions is high. To a large degree, this potential for accurate “reading” of ultrasonic diagnostic displays depends upon high resolution of the equipment as well as on the skill of the “reader.”

The 8085 microcomputer system runs 8080 programs without modification and is buscompatible with 8080 components. Upgrading includes a reduction in components - a typical three-chip 8085 system can replace up to ten or more 8080-system components. The operating rate with standard-speed memory is 3 MHz instead of 2 MHz; throughput can be increased 50 percent in some applications.

Five articles on power supply technology and selection This 14-page booklet contains five short articles on power supplies. The first, by Harry Taylor, discusses factors such as complexity, quantity, and cost evaluation, that bear on the make — buy decision for power supplies. William Pharmer then discusses the relative merits of custom and standard supplies. John Roland covers the specification of high-voltage power supplies with main emphasis on electrical performance, static loading conditions, environmental considerations, and mechanicals aspects. Oil as a high-voltage insulator is discussed by Meade Bierley, and high-voltage circuit packaging is covered by Jan Askman.

The basic operation of spectrum analyzers is explained and several applications are laid out in this 22-page brochure. In a question-and-answer format, the discussion first explains the value of preselection, and then considers intermods and the intermod performance of spectral analyzers. Phase lock is explained and the discussion of IF fitters includes material on shape factor. Limits and usefulness of dynamic range are covered. The discussion of sensitivity touches on minimum discernible signal and noise figures.

articleTitle: New product applications: Low-profile keyboard design can cut costs for x-y switching and interface layouts
abstract: Called the “X-Y Matrix,” this keyboard sells for 4 cents per switch position in quantities of 100 000. Prices are less for higher volumes. Originally developed for this manufacturer's calculators, the product is now offered for noncalculator applications such as credit-card verifiers, telephone data-handling equipment, electronic games, and other consumer products with digital control.

Britain's experimental fast breeder reactor at Dounreay, Scotland, has successfully completed a series of safety experiments, which culminated in a test in which the reactor coolant, liquid sodium, was deliberately stopped from circulating. During the test, the nuclear-fuel temperature exceeded 1000°C, causing the stainless-steel containers to melt, and although the fuel came into contact with the sodium coolant, no adverse affects have been reported. The 13-MW (electrical) reactor was completed in 1959. A second reactor, the 250-MW (e) prototype fast breeder reactor, also located at Dounreay, began delivering electric power to the United Kingdom in 1974.

This eight-page booklet explains the properties and characteristics of superconducting cables. Three cable materials - NbTi, Nb3Sn, and flexible Nb3Sn - are discussed. Composition, wire-filament size, operating temperatures, and other important parameters are covered. Relationship between minimum bend diameter and strand diameter, special production techniques, and critical currents are among the topics discussed for each material. A general discussion covers insulation, twisted filaments, mixed-matrix superconductors, multistrand conductors, mechanical properties, quality assurance, joining, and special superconductors.

The average monthly starting salary for new B.S.E.E. graduates during the 1976–1977 academic year was $1245, an increase of 8.6 percent over 1975–1976 figures, according to the College Placement Council's July 1977 report. Some other engineering specialties fared even better; chemical engineers were reported starting at $1389 per month, and mechanical engineers at $1286 per month. Lower monthly earnings were reported for industrial engineers ($1257), civil engineers ($1185), and graduates of four-year engineering technology programs ($1177).
